extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Andrew Carnegie's memoirs; readers interested in Gilded Age politics, diplomacy, and philanthropy
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from Andrew Carnegie's autobiographical chapters recounting episodes in U.S. diplomacy, statesmanship, and philanthropic decisions around the Harrison, Blaine, Hay, and McKinley administrations. Contains narrative plus normative comments about how statesmen and philanthropists ought to behave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect national feeling of neighboring republics
rubrics_metrics.description: “It will behoove subsequent governments to scrupulously respect the national feeling of our Southern neighbors. It is not control, but friendly coöperation upon terms of perfect equality we should seek.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie argues that the United States should avoid a 'big brother' posture toward South American republics and should pursue friendly cooperation founded on equality rather than control; recognize and respect their sensitive spirit of independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer arbitration and peace over resort to war
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated praise of Blaine as 'calm, wise, and peace-pursuing' and examples where calmer counsels prevailed to keep the United States out of foreign trouble (Behring Sea, quarrel with Chili).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diplomacy and arbitration where possible; able and willing statesmen should seek peaceful settlements even when provoked; avoid hasty military action (illustrated by Blaine's interventions and the adjustment of disputes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid territorial aggrandizement; keep promises of independence
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Government then announced that war was not undertaken for territorial aggrandizement, and Cuba was promised independence--a promise faithfully kept.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When engaging in conflict or intervention, avoid annexation/imperial expansion; uphold commitments made to subject peoples (Carnegie contrasts this with the stain left by possession of the Philippines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid distant possessions and the vortex of militarism
rubrics_metrics.description: On the Philippines annexation: it was a serious departure from the traditional policy of avoiding distant and disconnected possessions and keeping our empire within the continent, especially keeping it out of the vortex of militarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers should be wary of acquiring far-flung colonies that pull a nation into militarism and away from its traditional continental sphere; prefer restraint and avoidance of permanent overseas control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer public infrastructure investment to military spending
rubrics_metrics.description: “It was better to spend three or four hundred millions upon [the canal] than in building sea monsters of destruction to fight imaginary foes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in constructive public works (e.g., canals, libraries) rather than expensive naval armaments which may provoke arms races; infrastructure spending can be a productive alternative to military expenditures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philanthropy should aim at public good, not personal glorification
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie explains that his gift of libraries and institutes was intended for the good of the people of Pittsburgh rather than personal glorification; he renewed an offer despite suspicion because he sought public benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gifts by wealthy individuals should be directed to create lasting public institutions that elevate the community (libraries, galleries, museums) and should be pursued even in the face of suspicion about motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government spending on civic projects yields high public return; constitutional interpretation should be flexible
rubrics_metrics.description: “Little of the money spent by the Government yields so great a return. So expands our flexible constitution to meet the new wants of an expanding population. Let who will make the constitution if we of to-day are permitted to interpret it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support expenditure on civic infrastructure (e.g., freshwater works, libraries) as high-return public investments; allow flexible interpretation of constitutional powers to meet emerging needs of a growing nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statesmen should be sincere, inspire confidence, and be prudent in speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of John Hay: 'he inspired men with absolute confidence in his sincerity,' and of Blaine: 'never did I hear him tell a story or speak a word unsuitable for any...a delightful companion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public leaders should cultivate sincerity and the confidence of others, and exercise discretion so their words and stories are suitable for broad audiences—this builds trust and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperative, equal policing of shared resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Blaine's proposal that Britain and America should each place small vessels on the Behring Sea with equal rights to board or arrest fishing vessels—'in fact, a joint police force.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared international resources are best managed through cooperative, equal arrangements (joint policing/inspection) rather than unilateral or dominating measures; practical proposals can achieve just and brotherly compacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders should exercise restraint in matters of national honor
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie's admonition: 'No man can dishonor me except myself. Honor wounds must be self-inflicted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal and national pride should not drive impulsive or self-damaging actions; restraint preserves dignity and avoids self-inflicted humiliation or unnecessary escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointments and promotions should rest on perceived fitness and merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Example of Mr. Shiras's appointment to the Supreme Court: 'Mr. Shiras received the strong support of the best elements everywhere... if he had not found Mr. Shiras the very man he wanted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection for public office should be based on the appointee's qualifications and the appointing authority's conviction that the person is right for the role, rather than purely on recommendations or favoritism.
